Wanderlust
WON-der-lust
noun (Millennial slang)
A German compound, wandern (to hike, to roam) + Lust (desire, joy), borrowed into English in the early twentieth century for a strong desire to travel. It had a quiet life until the 2010s, when it became a defining Instagram hashtag and tattoo of Millennial travel culture: backpacking, solo trips, "wanderlust" captions under sunsets in Bali and Iceland, and a whole lifestyle of experiences over possessions.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wanderlust is the itch to travel: to see new places, to be on the road, to collect countries and sunsets. For Millennials it became an identity and an aesthetic, the backpack, the passport stamps, the caption under the cliff-edge photo. The Christian observation: the desire to see God’s world is good. "The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof" (Psa 24:1), and travel can open the eyes to His creativity and to the breadth of His people. Abraham went out "not knowing whither he went" (Heb 11:8), and the apostles crossed the known world. But Scripture distinguishes the pilgrim from the wanderer. The pilgrim travels toward a destination: the patriarchs "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth … they seek a country" (Heb 11:13-14). The wanderer simply moves. Scripture is not romantic about restless wandering. Cain was sentenced to be "a fugitive and a vagabond" (Gen 4:12); "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place" (Pro 27:8); and God said of a faithless people, "Thus have they loved to wander, they have not refrained their feet" (Jer 14:10). Wanderlust can be a symptom of a heart that has not found rest and hopes the next place will supply it. A father can take his children to see the world and teach them that the deepest longing behind wanderlust is a longing for home, the city with foundations whose builder and maker is God.

Webster 1828 Definition

German loan (early 20th c.) turned Millennial travel identity (2010s Instagram) for the strong desire to roam; seeing God’s world is good (Psa 24:1), but Scripture distinguishes the pilgrim seeking a country (Heb 11:13-14) from the restless wanderer (Pro 27:8).

WANDERLUST, n. (German loan, early 20th c.; Millennial travel culture, 2010s) A strong desire to travel and explore. Popular as a hashtag, caption, and tattoo; related travel bug, digital nomad.

Webster (1828), root wander: WANDER, verb intransitive [G., to wander to walk, to change, exchange or transform.] 1. To rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object in view; as, to wander over the fields; to wander about the town, or about the country. Men may sometimes wander for amusement or exercise. Persons sometimes wander because they have no home and are wretched, and sometimes because they have no occupation. They wandered about in sheep-skins and goat-skins. Hebrews 11:37 . He wandereth abroad for bread. Job 15:23 . […]

Decode for parents: travel well with your children, and teach them the difference between a pilgrim and a wanderer.

Key Scripture

Psa 24:1 — "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein."

Heb 11:13-14 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country."

Pro 27:8 — "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place."

Jer 14:10 — "Thus saith the LORD unto this people, Thus have they loved to wander, they have not refrained their feet, therefore the LORD doth not accept them; he will now remember their iniquity, and visit their sins."

Heb 11:10 — "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Modern Corruption

Wanderlust can be healthy delight in God’s world or a restless heart hoping the next place will bring rest; Scripture blesses the pilgrim and warns the wanderer.

expand to see more

The corruption is restlessness baptized as adventure. The Millennial travel aesthetic often sold movement as meaning: if life feels empty, go somewhere new. But the soul travels with the traveller. Augustine’s line is the diagnosis: our hearts are restless till they rest in God. A life of constant movement can also avoid the commitments that make a life: a church, a marriage, a neighbourhood, a vocation rooted in one place.

The redemption is pilgrimage. Abraham travelled because he "looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Heb 11:10). Christians can travel gladly, to see wonders, serve missions, and visit the Church around the world, while staying rooted in a local body and a home. Teach the young that the road is good when it leads somewhere, and that the true home they long for is not a place on the map but the presence of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

German wandern (to roam) + Lust (desire) → Wanderlust → English (early 20th c.) → 2010s Instagram travel identity.
